item.description: The Supreme Court won't let Donald Trump's post office decide who gets a mail ballot. A federal judge froze his Postal Service rule for this election, and Monday the Court refused to lift that freeze. The rule would have let the post office refuse any ballot from a voter the state had not first reported to a federal portal, and North Carolina mailed its ballots ten days ago. The states' lawsuit over whether the rule is legal at all continues in the lower courts after the election. Trump's most reliable allies, Justices Alito and Thomas, dissented. Justice Kavanaugh voted against him but wrote that the rule may well be legal, only too late for this election. I've emailed 9,091 stories over 592 straight nights, free and without ads. item.title: One of The Carol Burnett Show's most iconic and hilarious moments (from Wayback in 1976) - Made possible by the late great Bob Mackie
item.description:
From a sketch parodying Gone With the Wind... "Went with the Wind!" Carol's character (Starlett O'Hara) refashions a set of green velvet curtains into a dress to wear. The script called for the dress to be hanging off Burnett, but Mackie did not find it funny. He asked the art director for a real curtain rod and green fabric and made the dress on a mannequin. Burnett said that she came into costume fittings and when she saw the curtain rod she said it was the most brilliant sight gag ever. The laughter of the studio audience was so sustained that it had to be edited for broadcast. It was the longest-length audience reaction in the series' entire 11-year run
In 2009, Mackie and Burnett donated the dress to the National Museum of American History

item.description: The sealed-battery era is being forced to loosen its grip—but Europe’s 2027 rule is more nuanced than many headlines suggest. Beginning February 18, 2027, the European Union’s Batteries Regulation will require portable batteries inside many electronic products to be removable and replaceable by the end user. Removal must be possible with commercially available tools, without proprietary equipment, heat, or solvents. Manufacturers must also provide clear replacement instructions and cannot use software to block compatible batteries. However, this does not mean every new smartphone or tablet will suddenly return to the old snap-off battery cover. Smartphones and slate tablets are covered by separate EU ecodesign rules that already began applying in June 2025. The European Commission has clarified that these more specific requirements take priority over the general Batteries Regulation. Manufacturers effectively have two options: They can design the battery so an ordinary user can replace it using basic tools, or they can allow replacement by someone with basic repair knowledge while meeting stricter durability standards. Under the second route, the battery must retain at least 83% capacity after 500 charging cycles and 80% after 1,000 cycles, while the device must also meet specified protection standards. So professional battery replacement services will not disappear completely. Some devices may still require a repair technician, especially when manufacturers choose longer-lasting, more water-resistant designs instead of fully user-accessible batteries. Even so, the rules could make devices easier to repair, keep spare batteries available for longer and reduce the number of working phones discarded simply because their batteries have degraded. The EU specifically describes longer product life, greater reuse and reduced electronic waste as central goals of the regulation. The legislation only governs products placed on the European market. However, manufacturers may decide to use similar designs worldwide rather than producing entirely separate European models—potentially spreading the benefits beyond the EU...
